_comment: Science response garnishes v1. One-line asides appended to science answers ~20% of the time when the trigger matches.

garnishes.text: (light circles Earth 7.5 times every second — that's how fast c is)
(no one has ever reached absolute zero — only gotten within a billionth of a degree)
(if the Sun became a black hole, Earth's orbit would not change — gravity only cares about mass)
(the math works perfectly; the intuition does not)
(Newton invented calculus to do this physics — he was 24)
(1905 was Einstein's 'miracle year' — four papers, any one a Nobel)
(entropy is the only law of physics that knows which way time flows)
(photons have zero mass, but they push solar sails)
(on Mars you'd weigh about 38% of what you weigh on Earth)
(everything is a wave; everything is a particle; live with it)
(GPS would drift about 11 km per day without relativistic correction)
(Galileo timed his pendulum with his pulse — there were no clocks accurate enough)
(magnetism IS relativity — moving electric charges look magnetic to a stationary observer)
(without friction you couldn't walk, drive, or hold a cup)
(a lightning bolt heats air to ~30,000 K — five times the Sun's surface)
(118 confirmed elements; 94 occur naturally; the rest are made in labs)
(life is carbon-based because carbon makes four stable bonds and chains beautifully)
(water expands when it freezes — one of the few liquids that does)
(pH is a log scale: pH 4 is 10× more acidic than pH 5)
(noble gases are inert because their outer electron shells are full — perfectly content)
(catalysts speed reactions without being consumed — they show up, work, leave)
(one mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles — Avogadro's number)
(same element, different number of neutrons — same chemistry, different mass)
(your DNA, plastic bottles, and rubber bands are all polymers — long repeating chains)
(diamond is just carbon — same element as pencil graphite, very different arrangement)
(if you stretched out all the DNA in your body, it would reach the Sun and back ~600 times)
(your body has ~37 trillion cells, working in shifts)
(the powerhouse of the cell, as you knew, was once a free-living bacterium)
(natural selection is brutally simple: more babies than survive, the survivors had something useful)
(viruses aren't technically alive — they need a host to do anything at all)
(your brain runs on about 20 watts — a dim lightbulb's worth of power)
(your brain has ~86 billion neurons, with ~100 trillion connections between them)
(you have more bacterial cells than human cells, by a ratio of about 1.3 to 1)
(the human genome is 3 billion base pairs — about 750 megabytes if you wrote it as data)
(every oxygen molecule you breathe was made by a plant or an algae splitting water)
(the Sun is 99.86% of the solar system's mass — everything else is a rounding error)
(the Moon is slowly drifting away — about 3.8 cm per year)
(Mars's sky is butterscotch because of suspended iron dust)
(there are more galaxies in the observable universe than there are stars in the Milky Way)
(at the center is Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole about 4 million solar masses)
(one teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about 6 billion tons)
(inside a black hole, the math says space and time swap roles — falling in becomes inevitable like the future)
(the cosmic microwave background is the afterglow — light from when the universe was 380,000 years old)
(we've confirmed over 5,500 planets around other stars — most via the transit method)
(Voyager 1 left the solar system in 2012 and is still phoning home — 22 hours each way)
(we've mapped Mars and the Moon better than our own ocean floor)
(78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% argon and trace — basically nitrogen with some breathing gas mixed in)
(Mauna Loa is the largest volcano on Earth by volume — most of it is underwater)
(the Richter scale is logarithmic: a 7 is 10× the shaking of a 6, but releases ~32× the energy)
(we are technically still IN an ice age — anytime there are permanent ice sheets, it counts)
(the atomic number IS the proton count — that's the only thing that defines which element it is)
(electrons don't really orbit — they exist as probability clouds around the nucleus)
(for scale: a rifle bullet does about 1 km/s — astronomy moves a lot faster than that)
(if you want this explained at a different level, just ask)
(this gets weirder the more you learn about it — fair warning)
(want a worked example with numbers?)
(rabbit hole alert: this connects to about ten other interesting things)
(scientists were arguing about this less than a century ago)
(gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces by a mile — a fridge magnet beats the whole Earth)
(a photon has no mass and always travels at exactly c — it never speeds up or slows down in a vacuum)
(stretched out, the DNA in one of your cells is about two meters long — coiled into a nucleus you can't even see)
(electrons don't really orbit like planets — they're smeared into fuzzy probability clouds around the nucleus)
(atoms are mostly empty space — if the nucleus were a marble, the atom would be a sports stadium)
(light takes about 1.3 seconds to reach us from the Moon and 8 minutes from the Sun)
(energy is never created or destroyed — it just keeps changing costume)
(entropy is why your room messes up on its own but never tidies itself — the second law has opinions)
(water is one of the few things that expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats and ponds don't freeze solid)
(most of Earth's oxygen comes from ocean plankton, not forests)
(carbon bonds with itself so happily it's the backbone of every known form of life)
(hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe — about 90% of all atoms)
(helium was found on the Sun before it was found on Earth — that's why it's named after Helios)
(sound can't travel through space — there's no air to carry the wave, so the vacuum is truly silent)
(you can never get a single magnetic pole — cut a magnet in half and each piece grows a new north and south)
(temperature is really just how fast atoms are jiggling — heat is motion in disguise)
(the pH scale is logarithmic — each step is a 10x change, so pH 3 is a hundred times more acidic than pH 5)
(electrons in a wire drift slower than a snail — it's the electric field that travels near light speed)
(without friction you couldn't walk, hold anything, or even strike a match)
(the air is pressing on you with about 14.7 pounds per square inch — you just grew up pushing back)
(a single glass of water holds more molecules than there are glasses of water in all Earth's oceans)
(a proton is nearly 1,836 times heavier than an electron, yet they carry equal and opposite charge)
(a free neutron is unstable and decays in about 15 minutes, but inside a nucleus it can live forever)
(bananas are faintly radioactive thanks to potassium-40 — the dose even has a nickname, the banana equivalent)
(plasma is the most common state of matter in the universe — stars are giant balls of it)
(in the quantum world a particle can be in many places at once until you look — then it picks one)
(in a chemical reaction atoms are never destroyed, just rearranged — the bookkeeping always balances)
(table salt is made from sodium, which explodes in water, and chlorine, a poison gas — together they season your fries)
(metals conduct electricity because their outer electrons roam free in a shared sea)
(gas molecules zip around at hundreds of meters per second, bouncing off each other billions of times a second)
(a teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons — density taken to the extreme)
(mass and weight aren't the same — your mass stays put, but you'd weigh six times less on the Moon)
(science doesn't prove things absolutely — it just builds the best-tested explanation we have so far)
(every atom in your body heavier than hydrogen was forged inside a star — you're made of stardust, literally)
(the same physics that makes an apple fall keeps the Moon in orbit — Newton's quiet genius)
(your heart beats about 100,000 times a day and never once gets a coffee break)
(your brain has roughly 86 billion neurons — fewer than once thought, but still more than there are stars in the Milky Way)
(you're born with about 300 bones, but many fuse — adults end up with 206)
(your blood vessels laid end to end would wrap around the Earth more than twice)
(your body makes about 3.8 million new cells every second just to replace the ones that wear out)
(your body carries about as many bacterial cells as human ones — you're more of a walking ecosystem than a single creature)
(a virus isn't quite alive on its own — it can't do anything until it hijacks a living cell's machinery)
(evolution has no goal and no plan — it just keeps whatever happens to survive long enough to copy itself)
(photosynthesis builds plants mostly out of thin air — most of a tree's mass comes from carbon pulled from the sky, not the soil)
(mitochondria were once free-living bacteria — they still carry their own separate DNA inside your cells)
(an enzyme can speed up a reaction by millions of times, doing in a second what would otherwise take years)
(your immune system can recognize billions of different invaders — it keeps a molecular wanted-poster for each one)
(jellyfish have no brain, no heart, and no bones — they've been drifting along just fine for over 500 million years)
(an octopus has three hearts and blue blood, and two-thirds of its neurons live in its arms)
(tardigrades can survive boiling, freezing, the vacuum of space, and radiation that would flatten almost anything else)
(the Sun is so big you could fit about 1.3 million Earths inside it — and it's still just an average star)
(the Moon is drifting away from Earth about 3.8 cm a year — roughly as fast as your fingernails grow)
(Mars is home to Olympus Mons, a volcano nearly three times the height of Everest)
(Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm so big it could swallow the whole Earth)
(Saturn is so light for its size it would actually float if you found a bathtub big enough)
(a day on Venus lasts longer than its year — it spins slower than it orbits the Sun)
(the Milky Way and Andromeda are heading for a collision — but in about 4 billion years, so don't panic)
(when you look at distant stars you're seeing the past — some of that light left before humans existed)
(a comet's tail always points away from the Sun, not behind its motion — the solar wind blows it back)
